strengths: The paper targets an important gap: fine-grained bilingual vision-language alignment, especially for Chinese, where evaluation resources are relatively limited.
The empirical scope is broad, covering region-level understanding, bounding box classification, OVD, retrieval, classification, dense prediction, and LMM integration across many datasets.
Results are consistently strong. FG-CLIP 2 substantially improves over SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP, Chinese-CLIP/R2D2, and MetaCLIP 2 on many fine-grained and Chinese retrieval benchmarks.
The proposed Chinese evaluation resources, especially long-caption retrieval and BoxClass-CN, could be useful to the community if released with clear documentation and validation details.

The model design is pragmatic and well motivated: longer text support, bilingual data, region-text supervision, hard negatives, dense features, and additional ranking/text contrastive objectives align with the target capabilities.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. Much of the system combines existing ingredients from SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP, LongCLIP, FineHARD, CMR-style ranking losses, dense features, and large-scale bilingual data; TIC is the main new loss, but its conceptual and empirical contribution is relatively small.

Attribution of gains is under-supported. The ablation only removes LCMR and TIC, leaving unclear how much improvement comes from architecture changes, bilingual data scale, long-caption generation, region supervision, hard negatives, adaptive resolution, or model/data scale.

Reproducibility is limited by heavy reliance on large in-house Chinese datasets, in-house region-text data, generated captions, and very large compute. The paper gives only high-level dataset sizes and training settings, not enough filtering, sampling, prompt, deduplication, or quality-control detail for others to reproduce the core result.

The new benchmarks raise soundness concerns. LIT-CN uses LMM-generated captions, DCI/DOCCI-CN use LMM translation, and BoxClass-CN is automatically constructed with detector proposals and filtered using FG-CLIP similarity, which may bias evaluation toward the authors' model family and does not fully establish human-verified ground truth quality.

Potential train-test contamination is not addressed. The model trains on LAION-2B-derived data, large web/in-house data, and generated captions, while evaluation includes web-derived and caption-generated datasets; deduplication against evaluation sets is not discussed.

Some comparisons may be difficult to interpret because FG-CLIP 2 benefits from much larger/private bilingual training data and specialized fine-grained supervision, while baselines are not retrained under matched data/compute conditions.

The TIC loss is not deeply analyzed. Its formula appears to only push apart hard-negative text pairs without a positive text-text term, and the paper does not discuss stability, possible semantic over-separation, temperature/scaling choices, or sensitivity to the 0.95 threshold/top-k choices.

Ethics and limitations are thin. The paper does not adequately discuss copyright/privacy issues in web-scale and in-house data, demographic or cultural biases in Chinese/English datasets, risks from detection/localization misuse, or the effects of LMM-generated annotations.

strengths: The paper targets an important gap: fine-grained bilingual vision-language alignment, especially for Chinese long-caption retrieval and region-level evaluation, where existing benchmarks are limited.

The empirical scope is broad, covering retrieval, fine-grained region discrimination, bounding-box classification, open-vocabulary detection, segmentation, zero-shot classification, and LMM integration across multiple model scales.

The reported numbers are often strong, especially on Chinese long-caption retrieval and region-level tasks, and the benchmark construction effort could be useful if released with sufficient documentation and safeguards.
weaknesses: The central claims are not well isolated. FG-CLIP 2 changes many factors at once: SigLIP 2 initialization, longer text length, Gemma tokenizer, adaptive resolution, massive additional bilingual data, LMM-generated long captions, region supervision, FineHARD, CMR, and TIC. The ablation only removes CMR and TIC, so it does not establish which design choices drive the gains.

Reproducibility is weak. A large fraction of the training data is described only as 'in-house' 500M Chinese image-text pairs and 12M Chinese region-text pairs, with no collection, filtering, licensing, quality, or release details. The paper says code/model/benchmark will be released, but provides no concrete artifact or sufficient recipe to reproduce the results independently.

The new Chinese benchmarks may have serious validity and contamination concerns. LIT-CN uses LMM-generated captions; DCI-CN/DOCCI-CN are translated with the same broad class of tools used for training captions; BoxClass-CN is automatically generated from LAION using detector proposals and FG-CLIP filtering with a very low similarity threshold. There is little evidence of human validation scale, inter-annotator agreement, error rates, or train/test decontamination against the very large private and LAION-derived training mixture.

Comparisons are not fully convincing. Many baselines differ substantially in training data scale, language coverage, resolution, tokenizer, and initialization. The paper often frames gains as methodological superiority, but the evidence is confounded by much larger or different training corpora and by using newer pretrained SigLIP 2 weights.

The proposed TIC loss is under-specified and weakly justified. The formula appears to minimize a log-sum-exp over hard-negative text similarities without positives, temperature details, normalization discussion, or analysis of possible representation collapse/side effects. The claimed importance of TIC is also not strongly supported: FG-OVD Hard drops only 0.7 points without it, while some metrics barely move.

The limitations and ethics treatment are inadequate. The paper uses LAION, curated web images, large in-house datasets, LMM-generated captions, and bilingual data, but does not discuss privacy, copyright, consent, demographic/geographic bias, harmful content filtering, benchmark leakage, or risks in deploying retrieval/detection systems.

Presentation has avoidable issues that reduce confidence: several implementation details are vague, some references/citations appear malformed, table placement disrupts the narrative, there are typos, and the limitations section is essentially future work rather than a candid account of weaknesses.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-served problem: fine-grained bilingual vision-language alignment, especially for Chinese, where existing evaluations are mostly short-caption retrieval. The proposed Chinese long-caption retrieval datasets and BoxClass-CN benchmark are useful contributions beyond the model itself.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering 29 datasets and 8 task families including FG-OVD, region classification, open-vocabulary detection, English and Chinese retrieval, zero-shot classification, dense prediction, and LMM integration. FG-CLIP 2 shows consistent and often large gains, especially on fine-grained region tasks and Chinese long-caption retrieval.

The method is technically plausible and well-motivated. Combining global alignment, region-text supervision, hard negatives, cross-modal ranking, and the proposed textual intra-modal contrastive loss directly targets the stated failure modes of coarse CLIP-style training.

The paper includes useful implementation details such as model scales, initialization, sequence length, optimizers, batch sizes, hardware, precision, and training schedule. The planned release of model, code, and benchmark would make the work practically valuable to the community.

Presentation is generally clear. The paper explains the two-stage training setup, datasets, evaluation protocols, and downstream uses in a readable way, and the tables make the empirical story easy to follow.
weaknesses: A large fraction of the central improvement depends on non-public or weakly specified data: a 500M-pair in-house Chinese image-text dataset and a 12M-image in-house Chinese region-text dataset. Even with released weights, this substantially limits reproducibility and makes it difficult to separate algorithmic gains from data-scale and data-quality effects.

The ablation study is too narrow for the scope of the claims. It isolates only CMR and TIC on the base model, but does not ablate key design choices such as long-caption training, Chinese in-house data, region-text data, FineHARD negatives, data-adaptive resolution, extended context length, or individual Stage I vs Stage II contributions.

The new Chinese benchmarks are promising but may contain construction biases. LIT-CN uses LMM-generated captions, DCI-CN/DOCCI-CN use LMM translation, and BoxClass-CN uses automated detection plus filtering with FG-CLIP similarity. More human validation statistics, inter-annotator agreement, contamination checks, and baseline sensitivity analysis would strengthen confidence that the benchmark measures genuine fine-grained understanding rather than artifacts of the construction pipeline.

Some comparisons may not be fully controlled. FG-CLIP 2 differs from baselines in training data volume, bilingual coverage, sequence length, region supervision, and objective design, so the source of the gains is not always identifiable. Compute/data-matched comparisons against SigLIP 2 or FG-CLIP would make the empirical claims more decisive.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. Given the use of LAION-scale web data, in-house web-scale Chinese data, LMM-generated captions/translations, and potentially person-containing imagery, the paper should discuss data provenance, privacy, licensing, harmful content filtering, bias across languages/cultures, and risks from releasing stronger retrieval/localization models.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. The paper’s main novelty appears to be a strong integration and scaling of known ingredients, plus TIC and Chinese benchmark construction, rather than a fundamentally new modeling paradigm. This is still valuable, but the contribution is primarily empirical and infrastructural.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: fine-grained bilingual vision-language alignment, especially for Chinese region-level and long-caption understanding.

Empirical evaluation is unusually broad: 29 datasets across localization, retrieval, classification, dense prediction, OVD, and LMM transfer. The reported gains over SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP, Chinese-CLIP, R2D2, and Meta CLIP 2 are often large, especially on FG-OVD, bounding-box classification, Chinese long-caption retrieval, and LLaVA-style downstream benchmarks.

The paper contributes potentially useful resources beyond a model, including FineRegion-CN and Chinese evaluation suites such as LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, and BoxClass-CN. This is valuable for a space where evaluation coverage is currently thin.

The method is practical and mostly well described: two-stage training, longer text context, dense/ROI region features, hard negatives, TIC, and CMR are clear at a high level, and the appendices include training data summaries, implementation details, and some controlled retraining comparisons.

Ablations indicate that TIC and CMR contribute beyond the base fine-grained/global objectives, and the controlled Stage-II-only comparison helps partially separate architectural/objective effects from data effects.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate. The system is largely an engineering integration of SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP-style region and hard-negative supervision, long captions, bilingual data, and existing ranking/contrastive ideas. TIC is simple and only weakly isolated as a conceptual contribution.

Reproducibility is limited despite the release claim. The strongest model depends on a 500M-pair in-house Chinese dataset, large-scale LAION-derived enhanced captions, and very large compute. The manuscript does not provide enough detail on filtering, deduplication, data licensing, or exact construction to let others reproduce the central training recipe.

Several benchmark construction choices may inflate or confound results. LIT-CN captions are generated by Qwen2.5-VL, DCI-CN/DOCCI-CN are translated by an LMM, and BoxClass-CN is filtered using FG-CLIP similarity. This risks evaluating compatibility with synthetic/LMM caption style or prior model biases rather than robust human language grounding. Human validation is mentioned but not quantified.

The central performance claims are hard to attribute. There is no full ablation for major ingredients such as Stage-I bilingual scale, long-caption generation, FineRegion-CN, data-adaptive resolution, region embedding design, or the 500M in-house data. The ablation focuses mainly on TIC and CMR, whose individual effects are sometimes modest except for COCO80.

Fairness of comparisons is imperfect. Many baselines are not trained with comparable data scale or bilingual region supervision, and the controlled retraining experiment omits Stage-I pretraining due to compute constraints, so it does not fully support claims that the method rather than data scale drives the main SOTA results.

The TIC loss formulation and explanation are underdeveloped. It pushes apart hard negative text pairs but lacks a positive text relation in the term itself, and the paper does not analyze possible effects on semantic neighborhood structure, multilingual alignment, or text embedding calibration beyond visualization and task metrics.

Limitations and ethics treatment are inadequate for a web-scale bilingual data paper. The manuscript has only a brief future-work paragraph and does not seriously discuss privacy, copyright/licensing, demographic/geographic bias, harmful content filtering, annotation/translation errors, or the risks of releasing large web-derived region-text data.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: fine-grained bilingual vision-language alignment, especially for Chinese, where region-level and long-caption resources are comparatively underdeveloped.

The empirical scope is broad, covering retrieval, region classification, FG-OVD, open-vocabulary detection, segmentation, zero-shot classification, and LMM encoder substitution. The reported numbers are often strong relative to SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP, Chinese-CLIP, and MetaCLIP 2.
The proposed Chinese resources, if actually released and carefully documented, could be useful to the community: FineRegion-CN, LIT-CN, DCI-CN/DOCCI-CN, and BoxClass-CN address real evaluation gaps.

The paper includes some ablations for TIC/CMR losses, bilingual Stage-II data composition, and retrained baselines under matched Stage-II data, which is a good direction for isolating sources of improvement.
weaknesses: The central claims are not supported rigorously enough. The method is mostly a combination of SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP-style region supervision, long-caption training, hard negatives, and a CMR loss from prior work; the genuinely new technical component, TIC, appears small and is only weakly validated.

The TIC loss is under-specified and conceptually questionable. As written, it effectively penalizes similarity to selected hard negative texts without clear treatment of false negatives or semantically valid near-duplicates. The paper does not analyze whether the top-k text negatives include same-object/same-category captions, nor does it provide stability or failure analysis.

Ablations do not justify the full training recipe. The main ablation only removes TIC and CMR from a strong system; it does not isolate long captions, Chinese region data, FineHARD, FineRegion-CN, loss weights, data-adaptive resolution, or initialization effects. The reported TIC gains are also mixed: FG-OVD Hard improves only 0.7 points, Flickr/ImageNet barely change, while COCO box classification changes substantially without a convincing mechanism.

Fairness of comparisons is hard to assess. FG-CLIP 2 is trained on 1.6B English pairs, 850M Chinese pairs including a 500M in-house dataset, plus large region datasets, whereas many baselines likely use different data/compute. The retrained baseline appendix uses only Stage-II data and no Stage-I pretraining, which does not establish fairness for the main large-scale results.

Reproducibility is poor despite claims of release. The manuscript has blank Homepage/Code/Model&Dataset fields, relies on a 500M in-house Chinese dataset, gives limited data filtering details, and trains on very large proprietary/expensive compute. Many important details needed to reproduce the results are absent.

The new benchmarks may be contaminated or biased toward the authors' pipeline. LIT-CN uses LMM-generated captions; BoxClass-CN is constructed using detectors and filtered by FG-CLIP similarity, then evaluated on models in the same family. This risks benchmark/model circularity and inflated performance, yet there is no human validation rate, annotation quality study, leakage check, or bias analysis.

The paper repeatedly makes strong statements such as 'rigorous and comprehensive assessment' and 'state-of-the-art' without sufficient statistical support, confidence intervals, significance tests, or careful accounting for scale, data overlap, and benchmark construction.

Presentation quality is below the standard expected for a main-track paper. Several tables are cramped or malformed, some numbers run into method names, there are typos such as 'empoly', the limitations section is minimal, and the impact statement is boilerplate and uninformative.

Ethics and limitations are inadequately treated. The work uses massive web-scale data, LMM-generated captions, translated category schemas, and region annotations, but does not discuss copyright, consent, privacy, stereotypes, Chinese-language cultural bias, harmful retrieval behavior, or dataset filtering beyond high-level statements.
Overall, the paper may describe a useful engineering effort, but its novelty, reproducibility, benchmark validity, and evidential rigor are not sufficient for acceptance at ICML in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and useful problem: fine-grained bilingual vision-language alignment, especially for Chinese-English settings where existing fine-grained CLIP-style work is much thinner than in English.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing at a high level: 29 datasets across retrieval, localization, open-vocabulary detection, dense prediction, zero-shot classification, and LMM integration. The reported gains are often large, especially on FG-OVD, Chinese long-caption retrieval, and bounding-box classification.

The proposed resources are potentially valuable. FineRegion-CN and the Chinese evaluation suite, especially long-caption retrieval and BoxClass-CN, could help the community study non-English fine-grained multimodal alignment more rigorously.

The method is practically well motivated. Combining global alignment, region-text supervision, hard negatives, long captions, and bilingual data is a coherent recipe, and the paper shows that fine-grained alignment can transfer to downstream detection, segmentation, and LMM benchmarks.

The appendices include useful implementation details, data examples, controlled comparisons with retrained baselines, bilingual data ablations, and hyperparameter tuning information, which improves the paper’s credibility.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is moderate. FG-CLIP 2 largely combines known ingredients from SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP, region-level contrastive learning, hard-negative ranking, and long-caption training. The new TIC loss is simple and plausible, but the ablation shows relatively small gains on several fine-grained metrics, so the main contribution appears to be scale, curation, and engineering rather than a substantially new algorithm.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the release claims. A major part of the Chinese Stage-I training data is a 500M-pair in-house dataset, and the training requires very large compute. If the in-house data is not released or precisely documented, others may not be able to reproduce the central results or disentangle method gains from private data scale and quality.

Some benchmark construction choices risk circularity or bias. BoxClass-CN is filtered using FG-CLIP similarity, while the submitted model is a successor in the same family; this may favor the proposed approach or related models. The long-caption datasets also rely heavily on LMM-generated or translated captions, so benchmark quality and diversity need more human validation and error analysis.

The comparisons are not always fully controlled. Many baselines differ in backbone size, pretraining corpus, language coverage, resolution, and token length. The retrained-baseline appendix helps, but it uses only Stage-II data without Stage-I pretraining, which does not fully isolate the effects in the main model setting.

The ablation study is useful but incomplete. It does not thoroughly separate the effects of long captions, region data, bilingual Stage-I data, FineRegion-CN scale, adaptive resolution, extended context length, and each loss component under the full training recipe. This makes it hard to know which ingredients are essential versus incidental.

The limitations and ethics discussion are too thin for a model trained on massive web-scale data and LMM-generated captions. The paper should discuss data provenance, licensing/copyright, privacy, potential demographic or cultural bias in Chinese and English data, benchmark contamination, harmful retrieval/use cases, and whether any filtering or safety audits were performed.
